{{short description|Guarantees chords of length 1/n exist for functions satisfying certain conditions}}

[[File:Chord graph.png|thumb| A chord (in red) of length 0.3 on a sinusoidal function. The universal chord
theorem guarantees the existence of chords of length 1/''n'' for functions satisfying certain conditions.]]

In [[mathematical analysis]], the '''universal chord theorem''' states that if a [[Function (mathematics)|function]] ''f'' is [[Continuous function|continuous]] on [''a'',''b''] and satisfies <math> f(a) = f(b) </math>, then for every [[natural number]] <math>n</math>, there exists some <math> x \in [a,b] </math> such that <math> f(x) = f\left(x + \frac{b-a}{n}\right) </math>.<ref>Rosenbaum, J. T. (May, 1971) ''The American Mathematical Monthly'', Vol. 78, No. 5, pp. 509–513</ref>

==History==
The theorem was published by [[Paul Lévy (mathematician)|Paul Lévy]] in 1934 as a generalization of [[Rolle's theorem]].<ref>[[Paul Lévy (mathematician)|Paul Levy]], "Sur une Généralisation du Théorème de Rolle", C. R. Acad. Sci., Paris, 198 (1934) 424–425.</ref>

==Statement of the theorem==
Let <math> H(f) = \{ h \in [0, +\infty) : f(x) = f(x+h) \text{ for some } x \} </math> denote the '''chord set''' of the function ''f''. If ''f'' is a continuous function and <math> h \in H(f) </math>, then <math> \frac h n \in H(f)</math>
for all natural numbers ''n''.
<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Oxtoby|first1=J.C.|title=Horizontal Chord Theorems|journal=The American Mathematical Monthly|date=May 1978|volume=79|pages=468–475|doi=10.2307/2317564}}</ref>

==Case of ''n'' = 2==
The case when ''n'' = 2 can be considered an application of the [[Borsuk–Ulam theorem]] to the [[Number line|real line]]. It says that if <math> f(x) </math> is continuous on some
interval <math> I = [a,b] </math> with the condition that <math> f(a) = f(b) </math>, then there exists some <math> x \in [a,b] </math> such that <math> f(x) = f\left(x + \frac{b-a}{2}\right) </math>. 

In less generality, if <math>  f : [0,1] \rightarrow \R </math> is continuous and <math> f(0) = f(1) </math>, then there exists <math> x \in \left[0,\frac{1}{2}\right]</math> that satisfies <math> f(x) = f(x+1/2) </math>.

==Proof of ''n'' = 2==
Consider the function <math> g:\left[a, \dfrac{b+a}{2}\right]\to\mathbb{R}</math> defined by <math> g(x) = f\left(x+\dfrac{b-a}{2}\right) - f(x)</math>. Being the sum of two continuous functions, <math> g</math> is continuous, <math>g(a) + g\left(\dfrac{b+a}{2}\right) = f(b) - f(a) = 0</math>. It follows that <math> g(a)\cdot g\left(\dfrac{b+a}{2}\right)\le 0</math> and by applying the [[intermediate value theorem]], there exists <math> c\in \left[a, \dfrac{b+a}{2}\right]</math> such that <math> g(c) = 0</math>, so that <math> f(c) = f\left(c + \dfrac{b-a}{2}\right)</math>. This concludes the proof of the theorem for <math> n = 2</math>.

==Proof of general case==
The proof of the theorem in the general case is very similar to the proof for <math> n = 2</math>
Let <math>n</math> be a non negative integer, and consider the function <math> g:\left[a, b - \dfrac{b-a}{n}\right]\to\mathbb{R}</math> defined by <math> g(x) = f\left(x + \dfrac{b-a}{n}\right) - f(x)</math>. Being the sum of two continuous functions, <math> g</math> is continuous. Furthermore, <math> \sum_{k=0}^{n-1}g\left(a+k\cdot\dfrac{b-a}{n}\right) = 0</math>. It follows that there exists integers <math>i,j</math> such that <math> g\left(a+i\cdot\dfrac{b-a}{n}\right)\le 0\le g\left(a+j\cdot\dfrac{b-a}{n}\right)</math> 
The intermediate value theorems gives us ''c'' such that <math> g(c)=0</math> and the theorem follows.

==Counterexample for non-integer ''n''==
Let <math> r \in \mathbb{R} </math> be arbitrary, and consider the function <math> f : [0, 1] \to \mathbb{R} </math> defined by <math> f(x) = \sin^2\left(\frac{\pi x}{r}\right) - x\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi}{r}\right) </math>. It is immediate that <math> f </math> is continuous, and <math> f(0) = f(1) = 0 </math>. If some <math> x \in [0, 1] </math> satisfies <math> f(x) = f(x + r) </math>, then <math> r\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi}{r}\right) = 0</math> which implies that <math> r = \frac{1}{n} </math> for some integer <math> n </math>. Therefore the theorem does not hold for non-integer values of <math>n</math>. {{Citation needed|date=December 2025|reason=Supposedly this counterexample was given by Paul Levy, but I can't access his article proving the theorem to verify that he gave the counterexample in the same article.}}
